summary: Analyzes the state of the Internet's domain-based routing system, focusing on inter-domain routing and its relationship with intra-domain routing. It reviews it against RFC 1126 and other requirements and design efforts. Its status is historic.

eli5.summary: This is a report card on how routing between big networks works and where it falls short, compared with what people hoped for. It is historic.

questions: what is the history of inter-domain routing requirements
what are the problems with bgp routing
how does bgp meet rfc 1126 requirements
subtitle: How the current internet routing system measures up against its original requirements.

tldr.problem: The internet has grown exponentially since BGP was designed, and routing today faces stability, scalability, and policy challenges that the original requirements did not anticipate.
tldr.mechanism: This document analyzes how well BGP and inter-domain routing meet RFC 1126 (the original requirements that shaped BGP), then catalogs the problems operators face today and the historical alternatives that were considered.
tldr.outcome: The analysis shows BGP has met many original goals but struggles with convergence time, auto-aggregation, multi-homing, and maintaining stable routing as the network becomes denser and more policy-driven. It is Historic.

today: RFC 5773 is Historic, a record of routing research from the early 2000s. BGP remains the inter-domain routing protocol and continues to be extended. The problems identified remain relevant: convergence time, routing table bloat, policy coordination, and the mismatch between traffic engineering needs and what hop-by-hop routing provides. Work on securing BGP (RPKI/BGPSEC) and on future routing architectures (such as SCION) continues to address concerns raised in this document.

sections.title: Why Routing Changed
sections.content:
When the Internet began, routers were organized into administrative domains called Autonomous Systems (ASs), each run by a single operator. This separation allowed different operators to set their own routing policies while still connecting to a shared network. The original architects of BGP assumed the network would grow in a tree-like hierarchy, with one backbone and branches below it.

By the time this document was written in 2001 (updated through 2006), the network had exploded: it was no longer tree-like but a dense mesh, the number of Autonomous Systems had grown beyond predictions, and service providers needed unprecedented control over how traffic flowed through their networks. These changes meant many of the original assumptions about BGP no longer held true.
sections.eli5: The Internet's routing system was designed for a small, tree-shaped network. By 2001 it had become huge and densely connected, like a web instead of a tree, and the design was starting to break.

sections.title: The Original Requirements from RFC 1126
sections.content:
RFC 1126, published in 1989, laid out what a routing protocol needed to do: route to all reachable destinations, provide loop-free paths, scale to thousands of Autonomous Systems, allow each AS to operate autonomously, support multiple routing policies, and provide enough management information for operators to understand what was happening.

Surprisingly, when Yakov Rekhter (one of BGP's designers) reviewed this analysis, he noted that RFC 1126 had not actually guided BGP's development—BGP was designed independently. Yet, by accident or design, BGP has met many of these requirements, at least for unicast (one-to-one) traffic. The problem is that the network has evolved beyond what those requirements anticipated.
sections.eli5: In 1989, people wrote down what an internet routing system should do: find routes, avoid loops, scale up, let each network do its own thing, and be manageable. BGP ended up doing most of those things, but the world changed around it.

sections.title: Problems with BGP Today
sections.content:
The document catalogs more than a dozen major problems. Convergence and recovery are slow: when a link fails, it can take minutes for all routers to update their routing tables, during which traffic may be lost or misrouted. Auto-aggregation does not work in BGP, meaning that as networks become multi-homed (connected to multiple service providers), they advertise many small prefixes that cannot be automatically combined, bloating routing tables. Multi-homing itself is inefficient: a network that wants redundancy must advertise routes to multiple providers, but BGP's longest-prefix-match rule can force all traffic through one provider instead of load-balancing.

Other issues include lack of tools to check policy consistency between operators, difficulty detecting and avoiding routing loops during transient failures, the gap between inter-domain and intra-domain routing (they use different protocols and metrics), security vulnerabilities to misconfiguration and malicious routing announcements, and the fact that a mistake in one peripheral network can propagate globally and break routing everywhere.
sections.eli5: When something goes wrong on the internet, it takes a long time to fix. Networks trying to connect to multiple providers get inefficient routing. One network's mistake can break routing for everyone. And operators have almost no tools to check if their routing policies will clash with neighbors.

sections.title: Alternatives That Were Considered
sections.content:
Before BGP became the de facto standard, two other designs were seriously pursued. ISO's IDRP (Inter-Domain Routing Protocol) was more sophisticated than BGP: it included better policy mechanisms, explicit loop avoidance using full AD (Administrative Domain) paths, security features based on X.509 certificates, and support for QoS-sensitive routing. However, IDRP was built for the OSI protocol suite, and when the Internet chose TCP/IP over OSI, IDRP was abandoned.

Nimrod was a research architecture that tackled scalability in a fundamentally different way: it separated the address space from the routing space and aimed to dynamically control the amount of routing information in the network. Nimrod's ideas influenced both MPLS (which borrowed the concept of forwarding along well-known paths) and PNNI (the ATM routing protocol, which used abstract map exchange instead of traditional distance-vector or link-state routing). PNNI was the first deployed protocol to use abstract topological information for inter-domain routing, though it assumed all peers cooperate—an assumption the Internet's commercial reality does not support.
sections.eli5: Other routing systems were designed before BGP won: IDRP had better policy and security but was tied to a dead protocol suite. Nimrod and PNNI tried different ideas about how to control routing information, but neither displaced BGP.

sections.title: What Changed Since 2001
sections.content:
The document notes several major shifts in the network's shape. The connectivity between large service providers shifted from a tree structure to a dense mesh, as local peering and Internet exchanges became cheaper and more common. End-user networks increasingly used multi-homing for redundancy, which accelerated the depletion of 16-bit AS numbers and dramatically increased the number of prefixes in routing tables. Classless Inter-Domain Routing (CIDR) and prefix aggregation, which had helped limit routing table growth, became less effective.

At the time of writing, the "width" of the Internet in AS hops was around five, meaning that a packet often traversed only five Autonomous Systems to reach its destination. This dense connectivity undermines BGP's scalability assumptions. The document also references emerging research projects like DARPA's NewArch, which recognized that global requirements may not be uniform: different parts of the network might need different properties at different times.
sections.eli5: By 2001–2006, the network was much denser (lots of direct links between providers), more networks were multihomed, and the routing tables were getting much bigger. BGP's original assumptions were breaking down.
